lead: This is the Lenten reading par excellence: a whole foreign city turns to God at the preaching of a reluctant prophet. Jesus takes up that story and turns it toward his hearers: those people listened to Jonah, and someone greater than Jonah is here. The question for Lent is simple. Nineveh needed five Hebrew words; how many have I heard? The key words are turn, sign and greater.

set: The Book of Jonah is short and unlike the other prophets: it is a story about a prophet, not a collection of his sayings. A prophet named Jonah son of Amittai appears in 2 Kings 14:25, in the eighth century BC. Many Catholic scholars read the book as a teaching story, written later, after the exile. Its message stands in either case.

Nineveh was a capital of Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel, and it stood in Israel’s memory as a city of cruelty; the prophet Nahum sings of its fall (612 BC). Jonah has already fled from this mission once, and has been swallowed and brought back (chapters 1–2). Now comes the second call. Chapter 4 will show why he ran: he did not want these people forgiven.
str: vv. 1–3a: the second call, and this time Jonah goes.
vv. 3b–4: the great city and the very short sermon.
v. 5: the people believe and fast, from the greatest to the least.
vv. 6–9: the king and his decree.
v. 10: God sees, and does not do what he had said.
kw: The Old Testament’s great word for conversion. It is about direction: you were walking one way, and you turn around. Here it is used of the people (v. 8) and of God (v. 9).
From a verb meaning to overturn, used of Sodom (Genesis 19:25). But it can also mean to be changed, and many have noticed the double sense: Nineveh was indeed overturned in forty days, by conversion.

Said of God, this describes in human language his turning from a threat when people turn from their sin. Jeremiah states the rule: “if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will change my mind” (18:8).
vv: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time,
The God who gives a second chance to Nineveh has first given one to his own prophet.
Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!
In Hebrew the sermon is five words long. There is no call to repent and no offer of mercy in it. A note on the text. The Hebrew says forty days, while the Greek Old Testament says three.
And the people of Nineveh believed God;
They respond before the king does, and before anyone tells them what to do. Foreigners do at once what Israel’s prophet had run away from.
Who knows? God may relent and change his mind;

The king claims nothing. Repentance does not put God under an obligation; it hopes in his mercy. Joel uses the same words (Joel 2:14). Even the animals in sackcloth (v. 8), with their touch of humor, show how complete the turning was.
When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways,
God looks at what they did: not at the sackcloth, but at the turning from evil and violence (v. 8).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ call to conversion does not aim first at outward works, “sackcloth and ashes”, fasting and mortification, but at conversion of the heart; without this such works remain sterile, and true interior conversion in turn seeks expression in visible signs (CCC 1430). Lent is one of the Church’s seasons of penance (CCC 1438). The Syriac Churches, including our Syro-Malabar and Malankara brothers and sisters in Kerala, keep a special three-day fast in memory of the repentance of Nineveh, before Lent begins.

r.h: Something greater than Jonah is here
set: Luke’s setting explains the saying. Jesus has driven out a demon, some have said he does it by Beelzebul, and “others, to test him, kept demanding from him a sign from heaven” (11:16). Now, with the crowds growing, he answers. He has already given signs. The trouble is what the demand for one more sign hides.
“This generation” in the Gospels means those who refuse to hear, in that place and time. It is a warning to every listener in every age, not a verdict on a people (CCC 597–598).
str: v. 29: no sign but the sign of Jonah.
v. 30: Jonah was a sign to Nineveh; so the Son of Man will be.
v. 31: the queen of the South.
kw: A mark that points beyond itself. A sign demanded as proof is different from a sign received in faith.
The queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–13), who came from far away to test Solomon with hard questions. A foreign woman and a foreign city are the witnesses in this court.
The Greek is neuter: not “someone” but “something greater”. It points to what is happening among them in Jesus, greater than wisdom and greater than prophecy.
vv: For just as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so the Son of Man will be to this generation.

In Luke the sign is Jonah himself and his preaching; Luke says nothing here about the sea monster. Matthew draws out the three days and three nights (Matthew 12:40). The two fit together: the one who preaches is the one who will go down into death and rise.
The people of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it,
The picture is of a court. The foreigners stand as witnesses for the prosecution, not because they were holy, but because they repented.
because they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
The argument goes from the lesser to the greater. Nineveh had a reluctant prophet and no miracles. We have the Son of Man.
ch: The Catechism says that only the divine identity of Jesus’ person can justify a claim like “something greater than Jonah” and “greater than Solomon” (CCC 590). It also notes that Jesus speaks of the sign of Jonah when he announces his Resurrection on the third day (CCC 994). So the sign that the Lord gives his Church is the Paschal mystery itself, toward which all of Lent is walking.

qa: Scripture says both things. “God is not a human being, that he should lie, or a mortal, that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19), and also that God “changed his mind” about Nineveh (3:10). God’s will to save does not change. The threat was given so that it would never have to be carried out. When we change, we meet that same will as mercy instead of as judgment. Scripture’s human language tells us that God truly responds to his people.
study: Jonah ran from a mission because he did not want certain people forgiven. Is there anyone I secretly do not want God to forgive?
What “sign” am I waiting for before I turn to God in earnest? What has he already given me?
